title: Query transformation and fan-out
summary: Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a technique it calls query fan-out: issuing several related searches across subtopics and data sources. Google also says there are no extra requirements or special schema for these features, and a page must be indexed (and eligible to show with a snippet) to be a supporting link. Research and vendor docs describe the underlying ideas: HyDE has an instruction-following model generate a hypothetical document, and Azure AI Search describes breaking a complex query into parallel subqueries. These show methods, not how Google decomposes any given query. Treat any advice on 'ranking for sub-questions' as practitioner inference.
actions: Check that pages you want cited are indexed and not blocked by snippet controls (nosnippet, max-snippet 0).
Plan content around the subtopics a broad question naturally contains; this is practitioner inference, since Google does not publish its sub-queries.
Do not add special schema or 'fan-out markup'; Google says none is needed.
Treat HyDE and Azure subquery docs as explanations of the idea, not as proof of Google's behaviour.

myths.myth: You need special structured data to be picked up by query fan-out.
myths.correction: Google says there is no special schema.org structured data to add and no additional requirements.

myths.myth: The HyDE paper shows Google writes hypothetical documents for your queries.
myths.correction: The paper describes a method that generates a hypothetical document; no saved Google source says Google uses it.

items.prompt: What does Google call the technique in which AI Overviews and AI Mode may issue multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources?
items.explanation: Google's AI features page says both features may use a 'query fan-out' technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources.

items.prompt: According to Microsoft's Azure AI Search documentation, what does LLM-based query planning do?
options: A. Rewrites the titles of every page in the index first
B. Breaks a complex query into smaller, focused subqueries
C. Removes every filter and returns the whole index to the user
D. Blocks crawlers from reading the subqueries it creates
items.explanation: Correct: it breaks a complex query into smaller, focused subqueries (this describes Azure AI Search only). Wrong: 'Rewrites the titles of every page in the index first' - nothing like this is described. 'Removes every filter and returns the whole index to the user' - not described. 'Blocks crawlers from reading the subqueries it creates' - not described.

items.prompt: True or false: In HyDE, an instruction-following language model is instructed to generate a hypothetical document.
items.explanation: The paper describes instructing an instruction-following language model to generate a hypothetical document.

items.prompt: The HyDE paper warns that the hypothetical document is unreal and may contain what?
items.explanation: The paper says the hypothetical document captures relevance patterns but is unreal and may contain false details. This is why it is a retrieval aid, not an answer to publish.

items.prompt: A colleague says 'To be picked up by query fan-out, add FAQ markup for every sub-question, even where the answer is not shown on the page.' Which correction is best?
options: A. Google's AI features page says structured data should match the visible text, and no special schema is needed
B. Valid JSON-LD is enough, whether or not the answers are visible
C. Fan-out sub-questions each need their own schema type to qualify
D. FAQ markup is required before a page can be used by AI Mode
items.explanation: Correct: Google's AI features page lists making sure structured data matches the visible text on the page, and says there is no special schema.org structured data to add. Wrong: 'each sub-question needs its own schema type' - Google says no special schema is needed. 'Valid JSON-LD is enough' - the page asks for markup that matches visible text. 'FAQ markup is required' - Google states no additional requirements.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved sources?
options: A. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use query fan-out
B. Azure AI Search docs say its subqueries run in parallel
C. Google's fan-out writes hypothetical answers as HyDE does
D. Google says a page must be indexed to be a supporting link
items.explanation: Supported: Google says both AI features may use query fan-out (A); Azure docs say subqueries run in parallel (B); Google says a page must be indexed to be a supporting link (D). Unsupported: C - no saved source says Google's fan-out uses HyDE-style hypothetical documents; HyDE is a research method.

items.prompt: Hypothetical page: a guide to home solar panels covering cost, installation and incentives. A developer left a noindex tag on it. Per Google's AI features page, can it be shown as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode? Answer Yes or No.
items.explanation: Google says a page must be indexed to be eligible as a supporting link, and lists noindex among the controls that limit what Search shows. A noindex page does not meet the indexed requirement (practitioner inference on the noindex consequence; the indexed rule is Google's).

items.prompt: A memo says: 'Google's docs say AI Mode uses HyDE, so put a hypothetical answer paragraph at the top of every page.' What is the main error?
options: A. HyDE requires structured data before it can work at all
B. A research method is presented as Google's behaviour
C. AI Mode cannot cite any web pages as supporting links
D. Hypothetical text must always be hidden from the user
items.explanation: Correct: HyDE is a research paper's method, and no saved Google source says Google uses it; Google's page only says fan-out issues related searches. Wrong: 'HyDE needs structured data' - not claimed anywhere. 'AI Mode cannot cite pages' - Google describes supporting links. 'Hypothetical text must be hidden' - not addressed by any source.

items.prompt: Hypothetical site: a travel blog. Symptom: a thorough page covering visas, costs and seasons never shows as a supporting link. Evidence: (1) the page is indexed; (2) the CMS template adds a robots meta tag with nosnippet; (3) competitors without that tag appear. Question: what is the best next step?
options: A. Add fan-out schema markup to the page template and wait for a recrawl
B. Add a hidden block of hypothetical answer text to the page
C. Disallow Googlebot in robots.txt for the whole travel blog
D. Remove nosnippet from the template if AI features are wanted
items.explanation: Correct: Google says nosnippet prevents content being used as direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and eligibility needs the page to be indexed and snippet-eligible. Wrong: 'Add fan-out schema' - none exists or is needed. 'Add a hidden hypothetical-answer block' - HyDE is not documented as Google behaviour. 'Block Googlebot in robots.txt' - that restricts access, the opposite of the goal.

items.prompt: Hypothetical site: a home-improvement publisher. Symptom: pages on installation and incentives are not cited, though the cost page is. Evidence: (1) robots.txt contains Disallow: /guides/; (2) installation and incentives pages live under /guides/; (3) the cost page lives elsewhere. Question: what is the best action?
options: A. Remove the Disallow so Googlebot can access /guides/
B. Add special schema to the guides
C. Set max-snippet to 0 on the guides
D. Rewrite the guides as HyDE-style hypothetical documents
items.explanation: Correct: robots.txt tells crawlers which URLs they can access and Google says its robots.txt directives for Googlebot manage access, so the Disallow is the likely cause (not fully pinned: a disallowed URL can still be indexed if linked from other sites). Removing it lets Googlebot access the pages. Wrong: 'Add special schema' - none is needed. 'Set max-snippet to 0' - that limits snippet use. 'Rewrite as HyDE documents' - a research method, not a Google requirement.
